clue.text: Ring-bearer from the party.

parts.note: fro is the old word for from, as in 'to and fro'
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: Someone carrying a ring away from a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Tolkien's hobbit who carries the One Ring is the answer; 'the' is a link word joining the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Lord of the Rings this hobbit is the one entrusted with carrying the Ring to its destruction.

clue.text: Fire victim admits it wasn't so hot there.

definitions.text: Fire victim admits it wasn't so hot there

parts.words: Fire victim admits it wasn't so hot there
parts.note: the proverb has someone jump from a bad place into a worse one, the fire, so the victim admits the earlier spot was cooler

explanation.surface: Someone burnt in a blaze says their previous location had been cooler.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'out of the frying pan into the fire' means escaping one trouble only to land in a worse one.
explanation.definitionFit: The kitchen utensil is the starting point in the proverb about going from bad to worse into the fire.

clue.text: Valentine's. brother's alternative relationship

parts.note: or is the word that introduces an alternative
a son is a family relationship

explanation.surface: Valentine's brother has an unconventional relationship.
explanation.walkthrough: Valentine and Orson is a medieval romance about twin brothers, one raised at court and one by a bear.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old French romance the twin raised in the forest is the knight Valentine's sibling.

clue.text: The Open River Prelude

parts.note: overt means open, not concealed
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, England

explanation.surface: A golf tournament and a river serve as the opening act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Open' suggests the golf championship; it is OVERT. The Ure is a river in North Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestral introduction to an opera or longer musical work, played before it begins.

clue.text: One hard of hearing is not helped by a ventriloquist

definitions.text: One hard of hearing is not helped by a ventriloquist

parts.words: One hard of hearing is not helped by a ventriloquist
parts.note: a ventriloquist speaks without moving the lips, so someone who follows speech by watching mouths gets nothing from the act

explanation.surface: A deaf person gets no benefit from a ventriloquist's show.
explanation.definitionFit: A deaf person may understand speech by watching mouth movements, which a ventriloquist deliberately hides.

clue.text: Willingly complicate life

indicators.note: to complicate is to mix up, so the letters of the next word are jumbled

explanation.surface: Gladly making existence more difficult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complicate' rearranges LIFE.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adverb means gladly, as in 'I would as lief stay'.

clue.text: Holding back a penny first for saving

indicators.note: first puts the penny ahead of the word for holding back

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for a penny
reserving means keeping or holding back

explanation.surface: Keeping a penny aside before anything else, to save money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' puts P before RESERVING.
explanation.definitionFit: Saving and keeping something, as food is kept from spoiling, are both conservation.

clue.text: Secret observation of one inside slip-up

indicators.note: the word for one goes inside the turned word for a slip
in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a lapse is a slip or small error
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Watching covertly, with a person caught in an error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slip-up' looks like a single word for a mistake, but 'up' turns LAPSE into ESPAL, and 'inside' puts I in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Espial is the act of spying or watching without being seen.

clue.text: One convulsed with hiccups

parts.note: a hiccup is a spasm of the muscle under the lungs, so that muscle is the one convulsing

explanation.surface: A person shaken by a bout of hiccups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' seems to be a person, but it is the body part whose spasms cause hiccups.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiccups are caused by involuntary contractions of the dome-shaped muscle between chest and abdomen.

clue.text: If I were turned out of the in my petticoat" (Eliz I)

definitions.text: If I were turned out of the in my petticoat" (Eliz I)

parts.words: If I were turned out of the in my petticoat" (Eliz I)
parts.note: the missing word completes Elizabeth I's boast that, even expelled from her kingdom in her petticoat, she could live anywhere in Christendom

explanation.surface: A quotation from Queen Elizabeth I about being thrown out in her underskirt.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth I said that if turned out of her kingdom in her petticoat she was able to live in any place in Christendom; the blank is that kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: A kingdom, the domain a monarch rules, is what the queen imagined being expelled from.

clue.text: Late last Thursday

parts.note: read from a Friday, the late part of the day before is the previous day's evening

explanation.surface: Something happened late on Thursday last week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' suggests recently, but it means late in the day: if today is Friday, late Thursday is the evening of yesterday, an old poetic word.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic compound means the evening of the day before today.

clue.text: A place in Spain

parts.note: the Spanish word for a public square is also, in effect, a 'place' in the French sense of a square

explanation.surface: Some location or other in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place' is read as a town square, as in French place; the Spanish word for that square is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish town square or open public space, the equivalent of a French place.

clue.text: Age of one catcher in New York ?

indicators.note: the words before are set inside the abbreviation that follows

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a net is something that catches fish or butterflies

explanation.surface: Asking how old a baseball catcher in New York is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catcher' suggests a baseball player in a New York team, but it is a thing that catches; the question mark flags the misleading picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A number of years, here a very great age.

clue.text: They flew with one third of their wings

definitions.text: They flew with one third of their wings

parts.words: They flew with one third of their wings
parts.note: in Isaiah 6 the angels about the throne each have six wings, covering face and feet with two pairs and flying with the third

explanation.surface: Birds that fly using only a portion of their wings.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bible (Isaiah 6:2) describes these angels with six wings: 'with twain he did fly', so a third of the wings were for flight.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the six-winged angels of the highest order in Isaiah's vision.

clue.text: That 'vital envelope

parts.note: the life-giving layer of air wrapped around the earth is read as an envelope

explanation.surface: An important envelope in the post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Envelope' suggests stationery; here it is the layer of gases enveloping the earth, vital because we breathe it.
explanation.definitionFit: The layer of air surrounding the earth, essential to life, encloses the planet like a wrapper.

clue.text: Jive with a poet, right ? Or change to a poetaster

indicators.note: change tells the solver to rearrange the letters of the words before it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet dancing the jive, or a poet being told to switch to bad verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or change' is the anagram signal on JIVE, A, POET and R; 'to a' joins it to the definition: 'poetaster' is itself a disparaging word.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a poetaster is a slighting, belittling term for a writer of bad verse, an example of a disparaging word.

clue.text: Feasting off curdled milk ?

parts.note: junket is a dessert of milk set with rennet, so eating it reads as feasting

explanation.surface: Eating a meal of soured milk.
explanation.walkthrough: Junket is a sweet dish of milk curdled with rennet, and junketing means feasting or merrymaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Merrymaking and lavish eating share their name with the curds-and-milk dish.

clue.text: A worker, or his cards ?

explanation.surface: A labourer, or the cards he is playing.
explanation.definitionFit: A farm labourer is a hired worker; in card games the cards dealt to one player are held as a single set.

clue.text: The whippersnapper's only worth three ha'pence

definitions.text: The whippersnapper's only worth three ha'pence

parts.words: The whippersnapper's only worth three ha'pence
parts.note: the old word names both a small silver coin of three halfpence and an insignificant young fellow

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark that a cheeky youngster is worth very little.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha'penny was the old British halfpenny coin; this archaic word meant both a coin worth three of them and a little upstart.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic term means a puny, conceited young person and also a tiny sixteenth-century coin.

clue.text: A small pair may go over one's hand

parts.note: a brace is a pair, as of game birds
-let is a suffix meaning small, as in piglet

explanation.surface: A little couple might pass above someone's hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small' supplies the diminutive ending LET.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrist ornament is slipped on over the hand.

clue.text: A quarter to' one, the oysters' answer ?

parts.note: N, north, is one of the four quarters or cardinal points of the compass
taken as written

explanation.surface: At a quarter to one, what the oysters said in reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A quarter to one' looks like a time but is N attached to ONE. In Carroll's The Walrus and the Carpenter, 'answer came there none' because the oysters had all been eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lewis Carroll's poem the eaten oysters give no reply at all, so their answer is nothing.

clue.text: Rustic lent an ear

explanation.surface: A country person who listened carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Antony's speech in Julius Caesar begins 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears', so these were the people who lent an ear.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustic is someone living in rural parts; Antony's audience of fellow Romans were asked to lend him their ears.

clue.text: Venus, eg, only half upset by this roller

indicators.note: only the second half of the word for Venus is turned around

parts.note: Venus is an example of a planet

explanation.surface: The goddess of love is only partly troubled by this machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only half upset' turns the last half, NET, into TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: On a typewriter the cylinder the paper is wound round is the platen.

clue.text: What a dipsomaniac cat does partly covers the answer

explanation.surface: A drunken cat drinking too much, which partly covers the solution.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat that drinks to excess laps too much, 'over-laps'; 'the answer' is the subject of the second definition: the answer itself partly covers.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat drinking far too much laps over the limit; tiles or panels that extend partly across each other are said to overlap.

clue.text: Game the French might think shady ?

explanation.surface: A pastime the French might consider dubious.
explanation.walkthrough: Ombre is an old card game; the French word ombre means shade, so a French speaker might think it shady.
explanation.definitionFit: A seventeenth-century three-handed card game; in French the same word means shadow.

clue.text: Prime rascal, of course

parts.note: a scamp is a rascal or mischievous person
I, the Roman numeral one, is first or prime

explanation.surface: A thoroughly bad rascal, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally' but means a course at a meal; 'Prime' is first, the numeral I.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaded prawn tails served as a dish make up one course of a meal.

clue.text: She's a fairy queen, elevated in New York.

parts.note: Queen Mab is the fairy queen in Romeo and Juliet
the El is New York's elevated railway

explanation.surface: A woman who is fairy royalty, raised up in Manhattan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevated' is the El, New York's overhead railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so it can stand for 'she'.

clue.text: The book of doings

parts.note: the New Testament book recording the deeds of the apostles

explanation.surface: A record book of activities.
explanation.walkthrough: The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament; doings are deeds.
explanation.definitionFit: Deeds performed, and the Bible book of the apostles' deeds, share the name.

clue.text: About one pound but it's put up

indicators.note: the word but goes round or about the pieces for one and pound

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Costing about a pound, but it's been raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts BUT around I and L.
explanation.definitionFit: Something constructed or erected has been put up, like a house.

clue.text: Well-known brand (a mere catch)

explanation.surface: A famous trademark, which is only a small catch.
explanation.walkthrough: A brand is an old word for a sword; King Arthur's sword was thrown into the mere, where a hand rose from the lake and caught it.
explanation.definitionFit: King Arthur's famous sword, a brand in the poetic sense, was caught by the Lady of the Lake's hand in the mere.

clue.text: Contrives to make men like M'Andrew.

explanation.surface: Someone arranges matters to produce men like a certain Scot.
explanation.walkthrough: M'Andrew is the Scottish ship's engineer in Kipling's poem M'Andrew's Hymn.
explanation.definitionFit: To contrive is to plan or arrange something cleverly; Kipling's M'Andrew tends a ship's machinery in the engine room.

clue.text: Sign as solicitor for tenants

parts.note: solicitor means one who solicits, so the notice in a window is touting for people to rent the property

explanation.surface: A lawyer signing documents on behalf of renters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitor' suggests a lawyer, but here it means something that solicits: a notice in a window inviting people to rent.
explanation.definitionFit: The notice hung on a vacant property announces it is available to be rented.
